title: Metal & Kitchen Treasure Basket
strapline: Cold, shiny and clatteringly loud — a basket of real kitchen metal for a baby to weigh, mouth and bang.
intent: Give sitting babies the qualities plastic can never offer — the cold, the weight, the ring and clatter of real metal.
Feed reaching, grasping and transferring with objects that surprise the hands: a heavy little pan, a light tea strainer, a cool spoon.
Invite babies to make sound on purpose, banging spoon on tin and listening to what different metals say.
Build early comparing — heavy and light, cold and warming, dull and shiny — all through the hands and mouth.
Root the exploring in safety, with a key person low, close and unhurried while the baby researches.
implementation: Fill a sturdy basket with clean kitchen metal only: metal spoons, a small whisk, a tea strainer, a jelly mould, a garlic press, a little pan and lid, a stack of measuring cups.
Sit the baby steadily, basket within reach, and settle yourself on the floor alongside — present, quiet, not directing.
Let the banging happen; it is the research, not the nuisance — name it softly when the baby looks up ('that spoon is loud on the tin').
Watch which metal each baby returns to — the danglers want the chain of measuring spoons, the bangers want the pan.
Check daily for sharp edges, rust or loose rivets, keep everything generously bigger than a choke tube, and wash all mouthables after each session.
key_questions: Is the spoon cold on your cheek — your face says it is!
That was a big clatter — can you make the tin sing again?
The whisk is heavy and the strainer is light — can you feel the difference?
Which shiny thing is coming up to show me?
Where did the little cup go — is it hiding inside the big one?

impact.text: Babies reach into the basket, grasp the cold metal, pass it hand to hand and take it straight to the mouth to find out more.
Babies explore the metal with every sense — mouthing the spoon, pressing the cold strainer to a cheek, staring into the shine.
A baby bangs spoon on tin, stops to listen, and does it again — making the sound happen on purpose.
A baby works one object deeply — dropping the whisk, posting spoons into the pan, tipping the cups out again and again.
A baby holds the shiny mould up towards their key person, vocalising — sharing the discovery.
Because their key person stays calm and close, the baby explores the loud, cold basket freely and checks back with a glance.

enhancements: A knotted chain of measuring spoons for the danglers to swing and clink.
Nesting measuring cups so hiding-inside and lid-matching become the puzzle.
A single big pan and lid — the loudest, most satisfying instrument in the basket.
A muslin over the basket to lift and peep beneath — 'where has the whisk gone?'
A photo home for families: 'she chose the tea strainer every single time.'

playing_exploring: The baby chooses freely from the metal, following their own fascination with no right way to play.
Every sense is at work — objects are mouthed, banged, stroked and stared into.
active_learning: Babies persist at self-set problems — fitting the little cup inside the big, making the tin ring again.
creating_thinking: Babies experiment — will the strainer clatter like the spoon did? — and show delight when the world answers.
